content: This updated Cochrane review evaluates the role of adjuvant radiotherapy, including pelvic external beam radiotherapy (EBRT) and vaginal intracavity brachytherapy (VBT), in women with stage I endometrial cancer following hysterectomy. The review includes randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing post-operative radiotherapy (EBRT or VBT, or both) to no radiotherapy or VBT alone. The primary outcome assessed was overall survival, while secondary outcomes included endometrial cancer-related deaths, locoregional recurrence, and distant recurrence. The analysis incorporated data from eight trials, involving a total of 4,273 women. Seven trials compared EBRT with no EBRT (or VBT alone), and one trial compared VBT with no additional treatment. Six of the eight trials were deemed high quality. However, time-to-event data were not consistently available across all trials and outcomes. EBRT, with or without VBT, significantly reduced the risk of locoregional recurrence. Specifically, the hazard ratio (HR) for locoregional recurrence was 0.36 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.25 to 0.52) based on time-to-event data from five trials involving 2,965 women. Similarly, the risk ratio (RR) for locoregional recurrence was 0.33 (95% CI 0.23 to 0.47) based on dichotomous data from seven trials involving 3,628 women. However, this reduction in locoregional recurrence did not translate into improved overall survival (HR 0.99, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.20) or endometrial cancer-related survival (HR 0.96, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.28). Additionally, EBRT did not reduce the rates of distant recurrence (RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.35). In subgroup analyses, EBRT did not improve survival outcomes in either intermediate-risk or high-risk patients. However, the data for high-risk patients were limited, and a potential benefit of EBRT in this subgroup could not be excluded. One trial (PORTEC-2) compared EBRT with VBT in high-intermediate risk patients and found that VBT was effective in achieving vaginal control. The difference in locoregional relapse rates between VBT and EBRT was not statistically significant (5.1% vs. 2.1%; HR 2.08, 95% CI 0.71 to 6.09; P = 0.17). In low-risk patients (stage IA/B, grade 1/2), EBRT was associated with an increased risk of endometrial cancer-related deaths, including treatment-related deaths (RR 2.64, 95% CI 1.05 to 6.66). However, data on overall survival in this subgroup were insufficient, and the evidence was considered to be of low quality. EBRT was associated with significantly higher rates of severe acute toxicity (RR 4.68, 95% CI 1.35 to 16.16) and severe late toxicity (RR 2.58, 95% CI 1.61 to 4.11). Additionally, EBRT led to significant reductions in quality of life, as well as impaired rectal and bladder function, persisting more than 10 years after treatment (based on one trial involving 351 women). One trial comparing VBT with no additional treatment in women with low-risk lesions reported a non-significant reduction in locoregional recurrence in the VBT group (RR 0.39, 95% CI 0.14 to 1.09). There were no significant differences in survival outcomes in this trial. In conclusion, EBRT reduces the risk of locoregional recurrence in stage I endometrial cancer but does not improve overall survival or cancer-related survival. It is associated with significant morbidity, including acute and late toxicities, and a reduction in quality of life. For low-risk patients, EBRT may have a detrimental effect on survival outcomes. For intermediate to high-intermediate risk patients, VBT alone appears sufficient for achieving vaginal control. The evidence does not demonstrate a survival advantage for EBRT in high-risk patients, but further research is needed to clarify its role in this subgroup. Additionally, standardized definitions of risk categories are necessary to guide clinical practice.
